articles.title: Rihanna gave $1.75 million to buy cancer-treatment equipment for a Barbados hospital in memory of her grandmother; 14 years later, the oncology centre is still delivering radiotherapy and chemotherapy
articles.summary: In 2012, Rihanna donated $1.75 million worth of medical equipment to Barbados’ Queen Elizabeth Hospital in memory of her grandmother, Clara “Dolly”
articles.body: In 2012, Rihanna donated $1.75 million worth of medical equipment to Barbados’ Queen Elizabeth Hospital in memory of her grandmother, Clara “Dolly” Brathwaite, who died from cancer that June. The gift helped modernise the hospital’s cancer-care services, and the radiotherapy unit was renamed the Clara Brathwaite Centre for Oncology and Nuclear Medicine. According to the Los Angeles Times, Rihanna said the donation was her way of giving back to Barbados and helping the hospital continue its modernisation programme.Fourteen years later, the centre remains a vital part of cancer treatment in Barbados. The Queen Elizabeth Hospital says the Clara Brathwaite Centre provides radiotherapy, oncology, and nuclear medicine services to public and private patients, including people travelling from overseas for care. The donation’s lasting impact is visible not only in the equipment once purchased, but in the continuing services that support patients and families facing cancer.A gift inspired by lossRihanna’s grandmother, whom she called “Gran Gran Dolly,” died in June 2012 after battling cancer. Later that year, the singer marked the donation with a ceremony at Queen Elizabeth Hospital, where the radiotherapy unit was renamed in her grandmother’s honour. The $1.75 million contribution was directed toward medical equipment rather than a symbolic gesture. Rihanna said she believed the gift would have a major impact on the people of Barbados and that it was intended to save lives or extend them. Her decision reflected both personal grief and a desire to strengthen healthcare access on the island where she grew up. By naming the centre after Brathwaite, Rihanna also ensured that her grandmother’s memory would remain connected to care for other families facing similar losses.The Clara Brathwaite Centre TodayThe Clara Brathwaite Centre for Oncology and Nuclear Medicine is housed within Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Barbados. The hospital describes it as a provider of radiotherapy, oncology, and nuclear medical services for patients at the hospital, as well as private and public patients from Barbados and overseas. The centre treats a wide range of cancers, including breast, prostate, gynaecological, lung, brain, head and neck, gastrointestinal, and blood-related cancers, as per the hospital's website. It also offers care for children from birth to 16 years old through its paediatric cancer services. Patients receiving treatment may undergo radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or both, depending on their diagnosis and treatment plan. The centre also provides haematology services and therapy support, including physiotherapy and occupational therapy.Why radiotherapy mattersRadiotherapy uses targeted radiation to damage or destroy cancer cells while limiting harm to surrounding healthy tissue. It is a central treatment option for many cancers and can be used alone or alongside surgery, chemotherapy, and other therapies.The Queen Elizabeth Hospital says its Department of Radiotherapy is based in the Clara Brathwaite Centre and serves patients across the island. Its work includes treating cancers that affect the breast, prostate, lungs, brain, digestive system, skin, blood, and immune system.Access to radiotherapy is especially important in smaller countries, where patients may otherwise need to travel abroad for specialised treatment. A local centre can reduce travel burdens, help families stay close during treatment, and allow medical teams to provide continuity of care.A lasting contributionRihanna’s donation came at a time when Queen Elizabeth Hospital was pursuing modernisation. The singer described the contribution as assistance for that programme, and the hospital’s continuing use of the Clara Brathwaite Centre shows how a single major gift can support care long after the initial announcement.The centre is more than a treatment facility. The hospital describes it as a safe and welcoming environment for people affected by cancer, offering patients, families, friends, and carers access to support, information, practical help, and a place to talk.That broader support matters because cancer affects more than the person receiving treatment. Families often need guidance on appointments, side effects, emotional wellbeing, and practical decisions during an already stressful period.Ongoing care in 2026The centre continues to operate as a key part of Queen Elizabeth Hospital’s cancer services. In September 2026, the hospital announced that some outpatient services at the Clara Brathwaite Centre would be temporarily relocated for a comprehensive deep cleaning of the department. During that period, routine clinics, radiation oncology, and chemotherapy services were moved to temporary areas, with the hospital chapel serving as the main waiting area. The hospital said its oncology team contacted patients to confirm or reschedule appointments as needed. The temporary relocation was presented as a maintenance measure rather than a closure. articles.title: After flydubai incident, Air France follows Israel restrictions and bans Pakistani, Muslim-majority crew
articles.summary: Air France has confirmed it is complying with new Israeli restrictions that bar flight crew members from certain nationalities from operating flights to
articles.body: Air France has confirmed it is complying with new Israeli restrictions that bar flight crew members from certain nationalities from operating flights to Israel, a policy that reportedly affects citizens of 31 countries, most of them Muslim-majority nations, including Pakistan, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Algeria and Tunisia.“Like all airlines, Air France is required to comply with the entry regulations established by the authorities of the countries it serves, both for its customers and employees,” the airline told Al Jazeera in a statement.“The staff concerned have been informed of the new regulations implemented by the Israeli authorities for flights to Tel Aviv,” it added.Israel’s directive affects crew from 31 countriesAccording to Israeli broadcaster N12, Israel’s Ministry of transport and road safety informed foreign airlines on October 1 that pilots and cabin crew operating flights into Israeli airspace must not hold the nationality or dual nationality of countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel.The directive reportedly covers 31 countries, many of them Muslim-majority nations. The list includes Pakistan, Iran, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Algeria, Tunisia and Niger.The move came a day after an Omani co-pilot allegedly attempted to hijack a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv and crash it into Israel’s Ben Gurion airport on September 30, according to Emirati and Israeli authorities. The co-pilot is accused of attacking the aircraft’s Indian pilot, who has been recovering in hospital.The restrictions could affect dozens of airlines operating flights to, from or over Israel.Other airlines confirm receiving directiveCzech airline Smartwings confirmed it had received the Israeli directive, but said its operations had not been affected so far.“We received the directive from the Israeli authorities in September 2026. We have carefully reviewed the directive and continue to monitor and comply with all applicable requirements issued by the relevant authorities. At present, the directive does not have any impact on our operations, crew management procedures, or the deployment of crew members on flights to and from Israel,” Smartwings spokeswoman Vladimira Dufkova told Al Jazeera.United Airlines said it had nothing to share but did not confirm whether it had received the directive or changed crew assignments.An internal memo to Air France pilots and cabin crew, seen by French investigative publication Mediapart, warned that “failure to comply with this directive would expose Air France and the employee to potential sanctions”. However he memo could not be independently verified.The restrictions have raised concerns over possible discrimination against airline employees based on nationality and could expose carriers to legal challenges under French employment law, according to legal experts cited by Al Jazeera.Paris-based anti-discrimination lawyer Clara Gandin said the restrictions could put Air France at odds with French employment law by treating employees differently based on nationality.“The measure rests on a collective presumption which amounts to a discriminatory bias: Every national of these 31 countries, most of them Arab or Muslim-majority, is treated as a potential security threat,” Gandin told the outlet.“Article L1132-1 of the French Labour Code prohibits any discriminatory measure based on a person’s actual or perceived nationality, in particular regarding assignment, pay and discipline,” she added.Gandin said the policy could also amount to indirect discrimination based on origin and possibly perceived religion, given that most countries on the list are Arab or Muslim-majority.According to legal experts, Israel’s authority to regulate access to its airspace and territory raises a separate question from whether airlines complying with the directive could breach employment laws in their home countries.Vincent Correia, a professor of air law at McGill University in Canada, said international aviation law recognises state sovereignty over territorial airspace.He also pointed to Article 13 of the 1944 Chicago Convention, which allows countries to enforce rules governing the admission of passengers and crew.He said crew members from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel were already barred from flying there, making the new directive relevant mainly to dual nationals.Gandin, however, said a country’s authority to impose entry restrictions did not automatically exempt airlines from their obligations under applicable national laws.She said Air France could choose not to operate routes under the restrictions or challenge the directive through the French government, the French Civil Aviation Authority or the European Union.Affected employees could seek damages, while trade unions could initiate legal proceedings, she said. Gandin also warned that the policy could raise concerns under data protection laws if airlines collected information on employees’ nationality without a direct and necessary link to their jobs.According to Mediapart, Air France had considered asking crew members to voluntarily disclose whether they were affected by the directive.The Alter union, which represents flight deck crew, reportedly persuaded management not to proceed, arguing that the measure would amount to “discrimination based on nationality”.The wider impact on international airlines remains unclear. Correia warned that similar restrictions adopted by other countries could complicate crew scheduling and airline operations.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Robin Williams’ watches and artwork fetched $6.1 million at auction, with money going to arts scholarships, wounded veterans, disabled athletes and sick children
articles.summary: Robin Williams' personal collection of watches, artwork and Hollywood memorabilia fetched approximately $6.1 million at a Sotheby's auction in New York on
articles.body: Robin Williams' personal collection of watches, artwork and Hollywood memorabilia fetched approximately $6.1 million at a Sotheby's auction in New York on October 4, 2018, four years after the actor's death. Titled Creating a Stage: The Collection of Marsha and Robin Williams, the sale featured more than 300 lots collected by Williams and his former wife, Marsha Garces Williams, during their life together. The collection included personal watches, film-related objects, bicycles, furniture and works by prominent artists. The auction was also organised around a charitable purpose, with proceeds designated to support several organisations, including Juilliard, Wounded Warrior Project, the Challenged Athletes Foundation, the Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation and St. Jude Children's Research Hospital.Robin Williams’ personal collection spanned Hollywood and his personal interestsThe auction offered a glimpse into Williams' life beyond his screen performances. Alongside film memorabilia, it featured artwork, watches and objects reflecting his varied interests. Sotheby's reported that the sale generated $6,088,250, exceeding the auction's high presale estimate of $4.6 million.One of the collection's most notable features was its range, from objects associated with Williams' film career to works of art and items he had collected privately. The sale also included a Gryffindor robe worn by Daniel Radcliffe in Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone. The robe was among the advertised highlights of the auction, which brought together more than 300 lots.The watch from Dead Poets Society fetched $32,500One of the most striking results was a gold-plated Hamilton wristwatch worn by Williams in the 1989 film Dead Poets Society. The watch, associated with his role as English teacher John Keating, had an inscription on its caseback identifying the actor and the film. It sold for $32,500, far above its presale estimate of $1,000 to $2,000. The result demonstrated the value collectors placed on objects with a direct connection to Williams' performances. The actor's film memorabilia attracted interest because it linked personal possessions with scenes and characters familiar to audiences.A Good Will Hunting painting sold for $90,000Artwork connected to Williams' film career also attracted substantial bids. An original watercolour by director Gus Van Sant, featuring a man in a boat, sold for $90,000. The painting appeared in Good Will Hunting, the 1997 film in which Williams played therapist Sean Maguire opposite Matt Damon as Will Hunting.Van Sant had inscribed the artwork to Williams, making it both a personal possession and an object with a direct connection to the film. The painting's final price substantially exceeded its presale estimate of $1,000 to $1,500. Williams won the Academy Award for best supporting actor for his performance in the film.Proceeds supported education, veterans and healthcareThe auction was intended to benefit several charitable organisations supported by Williams and his family. They included the Juilliard School, where Williams studied, and the Wounded Warrior Project, which supports injured and ill military veterans. The Challenged Athletes Foundation, which helps people with physical disabilities participate in sports, was also among the beneficiaries.Other organisations included the Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation, which supports people living with paralysis and funds research, and St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, which focuses on childhood cancer and other life-threatening diseases. Human Rights Watch was also identified among the beneficiaries. The auction's charitable purpose reflected the couple's support for arts education, healthcare, disability-related causes and human rights.Juilliard scholarship continued Williams' legacyWilliams' connection to Juilliard was particularly personal. He attended the performing arts school in New York before pursuing his acting career. Following the auction, a portion of the proceeds helped establish the Robin Williams Scholarship Fund as a permanent endowment, supporting future students at the institution.The scholarship offered a lasting link between the actor's career and the school where he developed his craft. The auction therefore brought together two aspects of his legacy: the performances and personal objects that audiences associated with him, and the charitable support intended to benefit students and communities beyond Hollywood.You use AI every day. articles.summary: The US Justice Department has issued an ultimatum to California to verify a list of suspected noncitizen voters and ensure election integrity, warning of potential legal consequences for noncompliance. This directive reflects increased federal scrutiny over voter registration and allegations of noncitizen voting.
articles.body: The US Justice Department has given California officials 48 hours to review a list of people suspected of being non-US citizens who were sent mail-in ballots, warning that it could seek emergency legal action if the state does not comply, according to the letter reviewed by Reuters.Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter sent the letter to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber on Tuesday. It said federal authorities had shared a list of suspected noncitizens with officials in Los Angeles County on a password-protected thumb drive.The letter directs state officials to withhold ballots from those individuals until their citizenship status is verified. For ballots already issued, officials were instructed to keep returned ballots separate and refrain from counting those already submitted until citizenship had been determined.The department warned it would have “no choice but to seek emergency relief” if California officials failed to follow the instructions.“Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes,” McCotter wrote.Justice Department spokeswoman Kiersten Pels confirmed the letter in a statement to Reuters, saying the department would take “all necessary legal action to protect election integrity and ensure compliance with federal law”.The demand comes as the Trump administration increases pressure on states over allegations that non-US citizens are voting in US elections.Last month the news agency reported that software glitches and clerical mistakes had resulted in more than 30,000 noncitizens being added to voter registration lists across US states since 2000.The latest letter follows a series of actions by the Justice Department targeting state voter registration systems. articles.body: NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar met his Canadian counterpart Anita Anand in New Delhi on Wednesday to review bilateral relations, with discussions covering trade, investment, education, energy, defence and people-to-people exchanges.The two ministers also exchanged views on key regional and global developments and discussed ways to advance the Strategic Partnership between the two countries.“Delighted to meet FM @AnitaAnandMP of Canada in New Delhi today. Guided by our leadership and sustained engagement across government and industry, we are advancing our Strategic Partnership,” Jaishankar said in a post on X.The meeting follows Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's telephone conversation with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday, during which the two leaders agreed to build on the positive momentum in bilateral ties and pursue concrete outcomes across key areas of cooperation.PM Modi, Carney discuss trade, security and CEPAPM Modi said the two leaders had a “warm and productive conversation” and agreed to work towards tangible results in trade, energy, technology, security and people-to-people ties.“Together, India and Canada are contributing towards a more stable and prosperous world,” PM Modi added in his post on X.When asked about the conversation between both leaders, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal on Wednesday said, "Prime Minister Carney had visited India recently, I mean some months back, and there is a positive momentum in this particular relationship on various aspects of our bilateral cooperation, strategic partnership and its progress in the areas of trade, investment, energy, technology, security, all these aspects that came up for discussion when the two Prime Ministers had their conversation on the bilateral relationship. So that is where we are."According to a statement from the Canadian Prime Minister's Office, the leaders welcomed increased engagement over the past year and reaffirmed their commitment to conclude negotiations on the India-Canada Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) at the earliest opportunity.The agreement is intended to support efforts to double bilateral trade by 2030. The two leaders also welcomed the ongoing Team Canada Trade Mission to India and discussed the impact of geopolitical instability on the Indo-Pacific region, as well as the importance of trusted partners in energy and agriculture.They also welcomed a bilateral security dialogue held in India the previous week as part of ongoing security and law enforcement engagement at the national security adviser level. Confident that the CEPA will provide fresh momentum to bilateral trade and strengthen our economic partnership for shared prosperity,” Goyal said in a post on X.Sidhu is leading a Canadian corporate delegation of around 300 members on a visit to India, Canada's largest such delegation to the country in three decades.The delegation is exploring potential joint ventures across sectors including aerospace, clean energy, technology, life sciences, agri-food and forestry. Sidhu said Canada was also advancing CEPA negotiations to create more opportunities for Canadian businesses and workers.Anand's third visit to India since June 2025Anand arrived in India on Tuesday. The MEA described the visit as reflecting sustained high-level engagement and positive momentum in bilateral relations.“A warm welcome to the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Canada, Anita Anand, on her visit to India. articles.title: Meet M Thangaraj, the Tenkasi teacher who turned a village classroom into a mini government; students run education, health and agriculture ministries, while his methods have reached 50+ teachers
articles.summary: A lesson about the stars can become much more than a science class when a teacher knows how to bring learning to life.
articles.body: A lesson about the stars can become much more than a science class when a teacher knows how to bring learning to life. At Panchayat Union Primary School in Puliyampatti, M Thangaraj uses a projector to take children beyond their textbooks, introducing them to distant constellations and the Milky Way. For his students, the experience offers a glimpse of a world far bigger than the one they see around them every day.But the space lesson is only one part of Thangaraj’s approach to education. With more than two decades of teaching experience, he has worked to make his school a place where children participate actively, take responsibility and feel encouraged to pursue their ambitions. His efforts earned him the National Teachers’ Award in September 2026. From creating student leadership roles to mobilising community support for school facilities, Thangaraj’s work extends beyond teaching lessons. His larger focus is on helping children gain the confidence, skills and opportunities to continue their education.Giving children a voice in their own classroomInstead of making students passive listeners, Thangaraj gives them responsibilities that bring them into the everyday functioning of the school. Children take on roles as student-ministers for education, health, agriculture and food, learning to contribute to their shared environment. The agriculture minister helps look after crops such as leafy greens in the school garden. The education minister keeps track of classmates’ learning progress, while the health minister encourages cleanliness and hygiene. The food minister promotes healthy eating habits and reminds students not to waste food during lunch.These responsibilities give children opportunities to practise teamwork, accountability and leadership from an early age. Thangaraj also combines digital tools with activities that encourage children to participate rather than simply memorise information. His classroom has a smart television, a projector and digital learning materials. Students can scan QR codes displayed on the smart TV to access educational content.“Children are not made to simply memorise lessons. Storytelling, games, role play, flashcards, and activity-based learning are part of my teaching. One of the methods is allowing students to scan QR codes displayed on the smart TV and access learning materials.” Learning also reaches beyond conventional subjects. With support from college students, Thangaraj has organised a Coin Expo and a Robotic Expo. Children also participate in yoga, chess, carrom, Oyilattam and kabaddi, giving them opportunities to explore different interests and abilities.Turning the village into a learning spaceThangaraj’s efforts do not end at the school gate. He has involved parents, former students, volunteers, local residents and organisations in improving the learning environment and giving children access to better resources. Through community support and funds raised at an education festival, he mobilised educational resources worth Rs 2 lakh. Volunteers helped provide a smart digital classroom and uniforms for 108 students. Supporters also contributed to roof and flooring renovations worth Rs 2 lakh and donated furniture.Environmental awareness is another part of the school’s activities. Students have prepared and sown 1,330 seed balls in agricultural fields around the village. Saplings have also been planted on the school campus with the support of an environmental organisation. Through these activities, children get opportunities to engage with their surroundings and take part in environmental efforts.Thangaraj has also shared his classroom practices with other educators. He has trained more than 50 teachers from the Kuruvikulam, Vasudevanallur, Kadayanallur, Keezhapavur and Shengottai unions. He has served as a district resource person for school management committee meetings and the Illam Thedi Kalvi initiative.Addressing the barriers that keep children from learningEngaging lessons are only one part of a supportive school environment. Access to books, suitable facilities and basic amenities also matters, and Thangaraj has worked to address these needs. Through Samagra Shiksha funds, he helped initiate libraries worth Rs 20,000 each in nine government schools. He also brought the absence of proper toilets for girl students to the attention of the district collector. The issue resulted in the construction of toilets worth Rs 5 lakh.His work has also taken him beyond the classroom. He has spoken about child protection and girls’ education on Tirunelveli Radio and presented his teaching methods at Manonmaniam Sundaranar University. These efforts reflect the different needs that shape a child’s education, from engaging teaching methods to facilities that help students attend school in a safe and supportive setting.A teacher’s influence that lasts beyond schoolFor Thangaraj, the value of his work is also visible in what happens after students leave his classroom. Some of his former pupils are studying at Tirunelveli Government Engineering College, while others have pursued degrees and paramedical courses. Many are working towards becoming first-generation graduates in their families.Former student P Lingakani credits him with helping her make important decisions about her future. She recalled that he recognised her abilities and guided her in choosing a stream after Class 10. When her parents wanted her to marry after Class 12, Thangaraj persuaded them to let her attend college in Madurai, where she completed her degree. He later encouraged her to join an IAS coaching centre in Chennai.“Thangaraj sir identified my skills and asked me to choose the right stream in plus one. When I completed plus two, my parents wanted to get me married. However, sir convinced them to admit me to a college in Madurai, where I completed my degree. He motivated me to join an IAS coaching centre in Chennai. I am preparing for the civil services examination.”Lingakani’s experience shows how guidance from a teacher can influence decisions well beyond academic lessons. For a student navigating choices about higher education and a future career, that encouragement can help keep new possibilities open. Thangaraj’s work brings together classroom innovation, community participation and individual mentorship. The projector that introduces children to distant galaxies is one way of widening their horizons. Helping them stay in education, develop their abilities and imagine futures they may not have considered is another. His achievement lies in making both part of the same learning journey.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: A red Chicago Bulls jersey worn by Michael Jordan during Game 2 of the 1998 NBA Finals has sold privately for $14 million, setting a new record for
articles.body: A red Chicago Bulls jersey worn by Michael Jordan during Game 2 of the 1998 NBA Finals has sold privately for $14 million, setting a new record for basketball memorabilia. Pennsylvania-based Hunt Auctions announced the sale on October 12, 2026, and identified the buyer as Miami real estate investor Ron Firman. According to ABC News, the jersey is the one Jordan wore on June 5, 1998, when the Bulls defeated the Utah Jazz to even the championship series at one game apiece.The sale confirms that Jordan memorabilia has moved beyond the world of sports collecting and into the territory of major cultural assets. Hunt Auctions president David Hunt said Jordan’s importance in the memorabilia market has escalated into an elite asset class more commonly associated with iconic works of art.The jersey from game 2Jordan wore the red road jersey during Game 2 of the 1998 NBA Finals against the Utah Jazz. The Bulls won that game, tying the series after losing the opener, before going on to win the championship in six games. That series was Jordan’s sixth and final NBA championship with the Chicago Bulls. The 1997-98 season later became the subject of the 10-episode documentary series The Last Dance, released in 2020, which renewed global interest in Jordan’s final run with the Bulls, as per the report.The jersey was also autographed by Jordan, adding another layer of value for collectors. Hunt Auctions described it as a game-worn, autographed road jersey from the Finals, rather than a replica or a jersey worn only in practice.A clear chain of ownershipThe jersey entered a private collection in 2003, when it was originally purchased from the Bulls by a collector. Hunt Auctions says it has since remained within a concise chain of custody, changing hands only once from the original purchaser.That provenance is important in high-value sports memorabilia. Buyers are often willing to pay more for items with documented links to the athlete, the team, and the specific game in which they were used.For Firman, the purchase represents more than an investment in a rare object. “Michael Jordan was an incredibly talented player who is admired around the world... I’m very excited about the purchase,” Firman said in a news release distributed by the auction house.A record for basketball memorabiliaThe $14 million price makes the jersey the most expensive piece of basketball memorabilia ever sold. It also places it among the highest-priced game-worn jerseys in any sport. The only known game-worn jersey to sell for more is the Babe Ruth jersey worn during his famous “called shot” home run against the Chicago Cubs in Game 3 of the 1932 World Series. That jersey sold for $24.12 million in 2024, as per the report.Jordan’s jersey now sits ahead of other major basketball collectibles, including another 1998 Finals jersey that sold for about $12.3 million last month. The market for items connected to Jordan’s final championship season has become exceptionally strong.Jordan items keep breaking recordsThis is at least the third time a Michael Jordan jersey from the 1998 Finals has sold for $10 million or more. A jersey from Game 1 sold at auction for approximately $10.1 million in 2022, while a Game 3 jersey brought about $12.3 million in a sale last month, reported ABC News.Interest extends beyond jerseys. In 2023, a pair of Air Jordan sneakers worn by Jordan in Game 2 against the Jazz sold through Sotheby’s for $2.2 million. At the time, it was described as a new world record for the most valuable sneakers ever sold.The pattern shows how the final Bulls championship has become one of the most valuable chapters in sports collecting. Items tied to Jordan’s last season with Chicago carry both historical significance and the emotional weight of an era that many fans regard as the peak of basketball’s global popularity.Why this jersey is so valuableThe jersey’s value comes from several factors. It was worn in an NBA Finals game, connected to Jordan’s sixth championship, autographed by the player, and preserved with a clear ownership history.Jordan’s cultural status also matters. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest basketball players of all time, and his influence extends beyond sport into footwear, advertising, film, and global popular culture.The 1998 Finals carry particular significance because they marked the end of the Bulls’ second three-peat. Jordan’s final shot in Game 6, followed by Chicago’s championship win, remains one of the most recognisable moments in basketball history.A new benchmark for collectorsHunt Auctions described the sale as another benchmark for the memorabilia industry. The $14 million price suggests that rare, authenticated items from defining moments in sports history can now command prices comparable to fine art.For collectors, the sale reinforces the importance of provenance, condition, and cultural relevance. A jersey is not valuable simply because it is old or expensive; its worth rises when it can be tied directly to a legendary athlete and a historic performance.For basketball fans, the sale is another reminder of Jordan’s enduring appeal. Nearly three decades after he wore the jersey in Salt Lake City, a piece of fabric from that night has become a $14 million symbol of one of sport’s greatest careers.You use AI every day. articles.title: A man fell 30 feet into a freezing well, broke his back and foot; months later, he tracked down the firefighter who saved him
articles.summary: A freak accident left Jonno Stubbs, 61, trapped in a well at his property in Cheadle, Staffordshire, in February 2026.
articles.body: A freak accident left Jonno Stubbs, 61, trapped in a well at his property in Cheadle, Staffordshire, in February 2026. The fall left him with a broken back and foot, and he spent three weeks in hospital. During the rescue, firefighter Jack Gaskell, of Cheshire Fire and Rescue Service’s specialist Technical Rescue Unit, was lowered into the well to reach him and bring him to safety. Months later, Stubbs set out to find the firefighter who had helped save his life. On Monday, 14 September, the two met again at Knutsford Fire Station.How a 30-foot fall into a freezing well left Jonno Stubbs with a broken back and footStubbs was building a workshop for his motorcycles on February 1, 2026, when the accident happened. He told the BBC he had simply walked across his yard when the paved ground gave way and he dropped into an 18th-century well. “There was a big splash,” he said. He puts the fall at 50 feet, though Staffordshire Fire and Rescue Service described it as 30 feet on the day.Emergency services were called at about 8:40am. Three Staffordshire crews attended, along with a technical rescue unit from neighbouring Cheshire Fire and Rescue Service. Early statements from the ambulance service described only minor injuries, but Stubbs had broken his back and foot and was treated for hypothermia. He feared he would not survive.How firefighter Jack Gaskell helped rescue himThe depth and confined space of the well meant specialist rescuers were needed. Gaskell, called in to assist Staffordshire’s crews, first lowered a life jacket and a two-way radio to Stubbs. Stubbs recalls telling him over the radio that he was fading and had to be got out. The next thing he remembers is Gaskell beside him saying they were getting him out.Gaskell had been lowered on a rope attached to a triangular metal frame. Once beside Stubbs, he reassured him and fitted him with a rescue harness so he could be winched to the surface. Stubbs was brought out at about 10:35am, almost two hours after the alarm was raised, and assessed by ambulance crews at the scene.Three weeks in hospital and a difficult recoveryStubbs spent three weeks in hospital. He described the recovery to the BBC as “awful,” affecting him mentally as well as physically, and he faces a long road back. He is a JCB fork-lift truck driver.Stubbs spent months trying to find Gaskell so he could thank him in person. He arranged the meeting at Knutsford Fire Station, where, alongside Becci Fisher, he also met the wider crew. “If it wasn’t for them, I wouldn’t be sitting here today,” he said. He described the reunion as giving him “a little bit of closure.”Gaskell said that in 22 years in the fire service, no one he had rescued had ever reached out to find him. Being contacted, he said, meant a great deal. “We do this job to help people,” he added, but you rarely get the chance to see someone afterwards.A rescue that led to an unexpected friendshipIn February, Gaskell had been lowered into a well to reach a seriously injured man. In September, he met that man again outside an emergency and saw how far he had come. For Stubbs, finding his rescuer was a way to thank the people who had got him through one of the most frightening experiences of his life.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Sydney WFH trader fired after work laptop exposes his Singapore getaway, wins unfair dismissal case
articles.summary: A Sydney-based currency trader was fired after his employer discovered that he was working from a hotel in Singapore while claiming to be working from
articles.body: A Sydney-based currency trader was fired after his employer discovered that he was working from a hotel in Singapore while claiming to be working from home in Australia. Although a workplace tribunal found that Charles Graham had deliberately concealed his location and that the company had valid grounds to dismiss him, it also ruled that his employer failed to follow the proper procedure.Graham won an unfair dismissal case on October 7 but received only four weeks’ pay in lieu of notice, without reinstatement or additional compensation.The Fair Work Commission found that Graham had knowingly violated his employer’s policies by concealing his location. His employer, HIFX Australia, which operates under the trading name Xe, dismissed him on December 2, 2025, after tracing his work laptop to a hotel in Singapore on November 17, when he was supposed to be working from home in Sydney.Work from Bali, telling boss plumber work going on at homeThis was not the first time Graham had stretched the boundaries of remote work. He had previously worked from Bali while telling his manager that he needed to stay home for a plumber who was fixing recurring bathroom problems.In September 2025, Graham had asked Xe for permission to work from Singapore for a year. The company rejected the request, explaining that his position was based in Sydney and it did not have a licence to operate in Singapore.Graham worked from home for several weeks, citing an eye injury, before taking annual leave for a holiday. He was expected to return to work in November.On November 17, his first day back after the holiday, his manager, Abigail Plummer, contacted the IT department to investigate his whereabouts.“Our mate should be online today, first day since his holiday, so I will need your FBI skills,” she wrote in an email.The ensuing investigation revealed that Graham was in Singapore rather than Sydney, as he had led his employer to believe.Graham says partner's infection deferred return to AustraliaDefending his actions, Graham said his partner had developed a bacterial infection during their holiday, forcing them to postpone their return to Australia. He said he had intended to inform his manager about the delay but was overwhelmed by unread emails, incoming calls and a complaint from a high-value client.Xe rejected his explanation, saying the documents he provided did not adequately establish that his partner was unable to travel. The company also said he had failed to explain why he kept his location secret.The employer cited other instances of alleged workplace misconduct. After a mandatory policy requiring employees to attend the office three days a week was introduced, Graham had reportedly arrived late on several occasions, claiming he was unwell or occupied with household chores.Fair Work Commission commissioner Alana Matheson ruled that Graham’s concealment of his whereabouts demonstrated that he understood he needed approval to work overseas. She described his failure to disclose that he was in Singapore as deliberate dishonesty and agreed that Xe had a valid reason to dismiss him.However, the commission also identified shortcomings in the company’s handling of the dismissal. Internal messages discussing a “strategy” and suggesting that Graham should be given “a bit of hope to turn up to the meeting” raised concerns that the outcome might have been decided before he had been given a proper opportunity to respond.Matheson found that the company had failed to fully explain the case against Graham and give him an adequate opportunity to defend himself. The company’s failure to follow due process meant that the dismissal was unfair, despite the valid grounds for terminating his employment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2015, Tyler Perry acquired 330 acres of Atlanta’s former Fort McPherson Army base; 11 years later, the site has 12 sound stages, 40 historic buildings and 200 acres of green space
articles.summary: In 2015, media mogul Tyler Perry bought 330 acres of Atlanta’s former Fort McPherson Army base for $30 million.
articles.body: In 2015, media mogul Tyler Perry bought 330 acres of Atlanta’s former Fort McPherson Army base for $30 million. Eleven years later, the large site has become one of North America’s biggest production facilities. It has 12 purpose-built sound stages, 40 historic buildings protected under national heritage rules, and 200 acres of open green space. The project is one of Georgia’s most notable urban redevelopment efforts. It combines the facilities needed for major Hollywood productions with buildings and land that date back to the 19th century.Military roots dating to the nineteenth centuryThe land now home to Tyler Perry Studios has a history that stretches back nearly 200 years. According to information published by Tyler Perry Entertainment, the site was first used for military purposes as early as 1835. It later became a Confederate Army post during the American Civil War. After the Battle of Atlanta in 1864, Major General John A. Schofield suggested naming the post after Union Major General James Birdseye McPherson. McPherson was the highest-ranking Union officer killed in action during the Civil War. Before his death, he had led the Army of the Tennessee through several major campaigns, including Fort Henry, Fort Donelson, Shiloh and Vicksburg. Over the next century, Fort McPherson changed to meet the needs of major international conflicts. During the Spanish-American War, it served as a general hospital. Later, during the First World War, it became a major training site for about 20,000 recruits. The fort also held an internment camp for German prisoners of war, an officer training centre and a medical centre. The medical centre treated more than 10,000 wounded and sick military personnel.The multi-million dollar transactionThe military base officially closed in 2011. After its closure, local officials began looking for a workable plan to redevelop the large property in South Atlanta. According to a press release from the Mayor’s Office of the City of Atlanta, the board of the McPherson Implementing Local Redevelopment Authority (MILRA) approved a resolution allowing the authority to sign a memorandum of understanding to sell 330 acres of the former base to Tyler Perry Studios for $30 million. Under the agreement, MILRA would keep more than 144 acres of the full property for other economic development projects and community housing needs. At the time of the preliminary agreement, former Atlanta Mayor Kasim Reed spoke about the deal’s expected long-term benefits for the local economy. "I am pleased that we reached an agreement that will help create long-term job creation, business expansion and community investment in Fort McPherson and its surrounding communities," Reed said in the city’s official announcement. "I am confident that this kind of development will bring hundreds of permanent jobs into the area, and attract robust additional investment into the Southside of our city." Former Atlanta City Councilmember Joyce Sheperd also pointed to the community effort behind the redevelopment. In the same city announcement, she noted that local leaders wanted to turn the former military base into a major asset for the wider region.Heritage preservation meets modern productionThe property sale was completed in June 2015. As part of the purchase, Perry committed to protecting the site’s historic buildings and features. Forty buildings within Fort McPherson’s 33-acre historic district are listed on the National Register of Historic Places. "The closing of this deal represents the start of a new period of job creation, business expansion and community development in South Atlanta," Reed said in a statement published on the official Tyler Perry Studios platform. "I am looking forward to the day when Fort McPherson is a catalyst for change in one of our most important neighborhoods." Instead of tearing down the original buildings, the studio made the 19th-century brick quarters, officers’ homes and parade grounds part of its working film locations. Today, these historic structures serve as administrative offices and filming areas where productions can recreate scenes from earlier periods. The project also added modern production facilities. The 330-acre campus has 12 specially designed sound stages, with the largest covering 60,000 square feet. It also includes a 75,000-square-foot water tank, custom-built backlots that recreate city streets and suburban neighbourhoods, and 200 acres of protected green space.Economic surge in south AtlantaThe purchase marked a major expansion for Perry. He started his studio business in 2006 and bought a smaller production facility in Southwest Atlanta in 2008. "I am thrilled to have my vision for Tyler Perry Studios come to life in South Atlanta," Perry said in comments released by the City of Atlanta press office. "I believe Atlanta provides a wide array of talent. Every single person, from the skilled production crew, to the artists and entertainers, are a vital component to making our films and TV shows come to life." State tax policies also helped support the studio’s growth. In 2008, lawmakers introduced the Georgia Entertainment Industry Investment Act. The law offered tax credits of up to 30 percent for qualifying film, television and digital productions. City reports stated that Georgia’s entertainment industry generated more than $5 billion in economic impact by fiscal year 2014. To manage the growing number of film-related applications, Atlanta created a dedicated Office of Entertainment to help coordinate permits and local hiring. Looking back on his journey from his early days in theatre to owning one of the country’s leading production facilities, Perry thanked the people who had supported him. In a statement published by his production company, he shared his appreciation for the audience that had followed his career. "From the 30 people who showed up for my first play 20 years ago, to the millions who stand with me faithfully today, 'Thank you,'" Perry said. "This dream belongs to all of us."You use AI every day. articles.title: Blue drum murder case: From husband’s killing to death sentence for Muskan Rastogi, her lover, here's what happened
articles.summary: MEERUT: More than 19 months after merchant Navy officer Saurabh Rajput was murdered, his body dismembered and his remains concealed in a blue plastic drum
articles.body: MEERUT: More than 19 months after merchant Navy officer Saurabh Rajput was murdered, his body dismembered and his remains concealed in a blue plastic drum filled with cement, a Meerut court on Wednesday sentenced his wife Muskan Rastogi and her lover Sahil Shukla to death.The case, which came to light in March 2025, went through 126 court hearings and the examination of 22 prosecution witnesses before the district and sessions court convicted the two on September 30. The prosecution had sought the death penalty for both.How the murder came to lightRajput, 35, returned to Meerut from London on February 24-25, 2025. Muskan’s birthday was celebrated the following day.According to the prosecution, Muskan and Sahil drugged Rajput and stabbed him to death on March 4 before dismembering his body and placing the remains in a blue plastic drum filled with cement and sand.Investigators said the accused had initially considered disposing of the body in a suitcase but turned to the drum after they could not fit the remains inside it. The two then left for Himachal Pradesh.The crime came to light in mid-March after a foul smell emanating from the drum led to the discovery of Rajput’s remains on March 17.Muskan had allegedly told her maternal family about the murder, following which the police were approached. Muskan and Sahil were arrested on March 18 after returning from their trip.February 24-25, 2025: Saurabh Rajput returns to Meerut from London. Muskan Rastogi’s birthday is celebrated the following day.March 4, 2025: Muskan and Sahil Shukla allegedly drug Saurabh, stab him to death and dismember his body. His remains are packed into a blue drum with cement and sand. The duo leaves for Himachal Pradesh.Mid-March 2025: Muskan allegedly tells her maternal family about the murder. A police case follows, and Saurabh’s remains are recovered from the drum on March 17.March 18, 2025: Muskan and Sahil are arrested.March 19, 2025: A court sends the duo to 14 days of judicial custody.May 12, 2025: Police file a nearly 1,000-page chargesheet, including around 34 witness statements. The charges include murder and destruction of evidence.November 24, 2025: Muskan gives birth to a girl while in custody. She and the newborn are shifted to a women’s barrack. Saurabh’s family seeks a DNA test to establish the child’s paternity.March 2025-September 2026: The trial spans around 13 months, with 22 prosecution witnesses examined.September 17, 2026: Final arguments conclude, with the prosecution seeking the death penalty for both accused.September 30, 2026: Muskan and Sahil are convicted of murder and destruction of evidence. The court fixes October 14 for sentencing.October 14, 2026: A Meerut court sentences Muskan and Sahil to death.A chargesheet, forensic evidence and 22 witnessesPolice filed a chargesheet of nearly 1,000 pages on May 12, 2025. It included forensic reports, call detail records, CCTV footage and statements from people connected to the investigation.The prosecution examined 22 witnesses, including Rajput’s family members, a cab driver, a medical store owner and people who allegedly sold the knife, drum and cement used in the crime.Investigators also recorded statements from hotel staff in Shimla, Manali and Kasauli, where the accused allegedly stayed after the murder.Police said there was no eyewitness to the killing. The prosecution relied on the evidence collected during the investigation to establish the case against Muskan and Sahil.The trial lasted around 13 months and involved 126 hearings. Final arguments concluded on September 17, with the prosecution seeking the maximum punishment.Court convicts duo, awards death penaltyOn September 30, district and sessions judge Arvind Kumar Mishra convicted Muskan and Sahil of murder and destruction of evidence. The court then fixed October 14 for sentencing, allowing the two to make submissions on the punishment.Both appeared before the court through video conferencing during the proceedings.On Wednesday, the court sentenced them to death, with prosecution lawyer KK Chaubey saying the judge referred to the Mahabharata while observing that punishing the guilty in proportion to the intensity of their crime was also 'dharma'.The court also imposed fines of Rs 50,000 each for murder and Rs 20,000 each for destruction of evidence.Rajput’s mother, Renu Devi, had sought the death penalty after the conviction, saying the family had waited 18 months for justice.Following Wednesday’s verdict, she expressed gratitude and said she hoped the punishment would serve as a deterrent and spare other families similar trauma.The case became widely known as the “blue drum murder case” because of the manner in which Rajput’s remains were concealed.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Meerut | Silver Rate in Meerut | Bank Holidays in Meerut | Public Holidays in Meerut | Meerut AQI | Weather in Meerut | Petrol Price in Meerut | Diesel Price in Meerut | CNG Price in Meerut | LPG Price in MeerutStay updated with the latest Meerut news. articles.title: Delhi protests: Pakistan-linked handles under probe for fake claims of police firing
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Delhi Police is investigating social media handles allegedly spreading rumours and inflammatory content during protests demanding Chief
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Delhi Police is investigating social media handles allegedly spreading rumours and inflammatory content during protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation in the national capital. The probe has traced the IP address of at least one suspicious handle to Pakistan, police said on Wednesday.Sanjay Bhatia, Additional Commissioner of Police in the Delhi Police’s Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit said that false claims about police action against demonstrators were circulated online to create panic and provoke unrest.The Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit has a dedicated cyber patrolling team to monitor such content and verify its authenticity, Bhatia told ANI, outlining the police's response to misleading posts."Delhi Police’s IFSO unit has a dedicated cyber patrolling team that monitors such posts to verify their authenticity and compliance with legal provisions. If we find a post to be factually incorrect, false, a rumor, a threat to public order, defamatory, or likely to incite anarchy, we take action in accordance with the law," he said.Bhatia said the investigation into the Pakistan-linked account was ongoing, along with other cases registered over social media content."When we sought registration details for one such specific handle, the IP address traced back to Pakistan; we are currently investigating that case. The process is ongoing, and we have registered other cases as well; investigations are underway, and we will share further details and evidence with you as they emerge," he said.Giving details of a post that allegedly claimed police were firing at demonstrators, Bhatia said the claim was false and could have heightened tensions."We found a post intended to incite chaos; the handle registered in Pakistan."He further claimed that the handle alleged that the police were opening fire on the demonstrators. "It was a deliberate attempt to whip up a volatile atmosphere based on falsehoods. Since the claim was untrue, we immediately requested the post's removal and registered a case; further action is underway," he said.The Delhi Police had also recently debunked a viral social media video claiming that Rahul Gandhi's residence had come under attack and that gunfire had been reported.According to the police, the footage was from December 2019 and was unrelated to current events. The police said legal action was being initiated against accounts sharing the misleading content and urged users not to circulate unverified videos.The investigation comes amid police action against three Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists over alleged attempts to disturb public peace and instigate others through social media. Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were remanded to five days of judicial custody, while Ajinkya Shinde was bound down for six months to maintain peace and good behaviour.According to a Delhi Police statement, the action followed an incident on October 13 in which the three activists and 11 other CJP members allegedly entered the denotified Jantar Mantar protest site through private premises and obstructed police personnel. articles.title: A Houston mansion built in the 1890s and expanded into a 36-room Tudor-style home in 1926 has been sold to a new owner; preservationists warn that it has no landmark protection and its future remains uncertain
articles.summary: Few buildings in downtown Houston look like the Kirby Mansion.
articles.body: Few buildings in downtown Houston look like the Kirby Mansion. Its red-brick walls, tall chimneys and steep roof, rising above the towers, are unlike anything else in the neighbourhood. Recently, the century-old, castle-like mansion at 2000 Smith St. changed hands. On 1 October, the historic mansion was sold to OB Texas Properties LLC, as reported by Chron. It is one of the last surviving grand homes of old Houston, and preservationists are now worried about its future. “We’re really concerned about the future of this building. We obviously want to see the building retained and put to productive use,” Jim Parsons, programme and communications director for Preservation Houston, told the outlet.A mansion from another eraThe mansion was originally built in the 1890s for businessman J.S. Price. Later, lumber magnate John Henry Kirby bought the property. Kirby, nicknamed the ‘Prince of the Pines’, is the namesake of Kirby Drive. In 1926, architect James Ruskin Bailey transformed the home into the sprawling, 36-room Tudor Revival-style residence it is today.In the 1800s and early 1900s, the area was called the South End, and it was one of Houston’s wealthiest neighbourhoods. Blocks of elaborate mansions and gardens once filled the area. Most have since been torn down, leaving Kirby Mansion as the largest surviving home from that bygone era.For the neighbourhood, this Tudor Revival mansion is a reminder of its grand past. “It gives us an idea of what the neighbourhood used to be like,” Parsons said. Now, preservationists are worried about its future.The sale that worries preservationistsThe Kirby family owned the house until the late 1940s. Later, the Houston-Harris County Red Cross used it as its headquarters for about 30 years, after which it became office space. In 2018, car dealer Ricardo Weitz bought the property. He considered building a Cadillac dealership on the site, partly because the house is visible from the nearby Pierce Elevated. That plan never materialised, and the mansion has sat mostly empty for years.Now, OB Texas Properties LLC owns the property. In a Facebook post shared on 6 October, Preservation Houston raised the alarm. “The building currently has no local, state or federal historic designation, which makes this an important moment for its future. We believe the mansion should be preserved and returned to productive use,” the organisation said. It also shared that it was in talks with the new owner and looked forward to meeting with them “to learn more about their plans and discuss potential preservation incentives that could support the building’s future”.Many residents commented on the post, shared memories of the house and said they hoped it would survive. “I was born at St. Joseph’s Hospital in 1947, like many Houstonians at that time, and remember the Kirby Mansion as one of the standout places that was Houston at the turn of the 20th century. A grand structure that must be preserved. Many of the magnificent homes that were surrounding this one are already gone,” one netizen commented. Another echoed the sentiment: “I’d noticed it from the highway for so many years and recently drove by it several times to take it in. It’s amazing, and the history is fantastic. I hope it is preserved!”Many netizens also speculated that the property could become a petrol station or convenience store. Parsons said companies linked to the buyer received permits in March and April 2026 to sell alcohol and retail hemp products at the address. Those permits, however, do not reveal what the owner intends to do with the building.“Beyond the fact that the permits exist, we don’t know,” Parsons said.As the mansion has no local, state or federal historic designation, it has no legal protection against demolition. Parsons said previous owners had never pursued such a designation, even after talks with Preservation Houston.Many people assume old buildings are automatically protected, Parsons said. The house could become offices, a restaurant, a hotel or another commercial space, Parsons said. articles.title: Ukraine says SpaceX limiting Starlink operations, impacting air defense
articles.summary: Ukraine is raising alarm that air defense operations are being impacted by unannounced limitations on SpaceX satellites. The disruption comes following Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warning that President Trump has threatened to cut off intelligence sharing with the country. Limits on Starlink’s services in Ukraine occurred without warning, presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram,…
articles.body:
Ukraine is raising alarm that air defense operations are being impacted by unannounced limitations on SpaceX satellites .

The disruption comes following Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warning that President Trump has threatened to cut off intelligence sharing with the country.

Limits on Starlink’s services in Ukraine occurred without warning, presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram, as reported by Reuters .

A source familiar with the matter told The Hill that Ukrainian drones, airplanes and helicopters were impacted by the limitations, with Starlink services cut off for objects that traveled faster than 100 miles per hour.

This hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept and counter Russian-launched explosive drones , the source said. Military units also reported issues with drone operations at lower speeds as well, the source said.

“This will also give Russians a real leverage on a frontline at the time when we effectively stopped their advances, and de-occupy the territories,” they added.

Ukraine uses Starshield, the military-grade network of satellite services provided by Starlink. The satellite internet provider is owned by Elon Musk, a tech billionaire and close ally to Trump.

SpaceX, which operates Starlink and is owned by Musk, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The slowdown in Starlink’s speed comes as the Trump administration is exercising renewed pressure on Zelensky, with Trump demanding Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries that he says are contributing to higher diesel prices in the U.S.

Zelensky told NPR in an interview published Tuesday that the president floated blocking intelligence sharing with Kyiv until it halted its strikes.

“Did we get any messages it can be stopped? Yes. My generals told me we have such risk,” he told the radio program .

The Ukrainian leader added that U.S. intelligence is important for receiving warnings about Russian ballistic missile strikes. Underscoring the threat, he said the nation had not received information about such threats over the last two nights, describing it as a technical glitch.

He did not comment on whether the U.S. was withholding the data.

Zelensky has defended strikes on Russian energy infrastructure as defensive responses to Russian attacks against Ukraine’s electricity grids and civilian infrastructure.

The leader also told NPR that he found out about Trump’s proposed energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine through the president’s social media account.

He also told Fox News on Monday that Kyiv held off on striking Russian energy sites following Trump’s directive, but that Russia hit Ukrainian gas stations , energy infrastructure and other facilities.

articles.title: Pope Leo recovering well after cancer surgery, Vatican says
articles.summary: The 71-year-old pontiff is recovering in Rome’s Gemelli hospital after surgery to remove a cancerous growth on his lung.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV is out of bed, walking, eating and has undergone respiratory physiotherapy, according to a doctor’s note published by the Vatican a day after his lung cancer surgery.

A blood test and chest X-ray revealed “normal post-operative” progress, doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora said, adding that values were “within the expected range for the type of procedure performed”.

“The Holy Father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room”, they said, adding that “he resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch.”

“Recovery is proceeding as planned,” the doctors said.

The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with cancer after an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, according to a medical bulletin published by the Vatican on Tuesday.

Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican added, noting the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests. It did not provide details on the recovery outlook or course of treatment.

The Vatican said the procedure lasted 90 minutes and that the surgery “was successful, and there were no complications”.

A medical statement shared by The Holy See’s press office, following the surgery, noted the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in the hope of eliminating any lingering traces of the cancer.

After the procedure, Pope Leo returned to his room at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where he is expected to recover for a week, with all his audiences through October 20 cancelled.

The Vatican said doctors are not currently discussing chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of other tests.

articles.title: Usha Vance, please speak up: Indians are not ‘indentured servants’
articles.summary: For Indians, the phrase indentured servant is not an ordinary political insult.
articles.body:
Vice President JD Vance has a legitimate argument to make about the H-1B visa program. But the messaging is off.

American workers deserve protection from employers who use immigration to suppress wages, circumvent fair hiring practices and replace domestic employees with cheaper labor. But when Vance describes H-1B workers as “indentured servants,” he crosses a line between criticizing a policy and demeaning the people who participate in it.

His wife, Usha Vance, has an opportunity to remind him, and the country, that Indian professionals are not a class of people whose contributions can be dismissed through such careless language.

Mrs. Vance is an accomplished attorney who has built her own professional career. Her Indian heritage is part of her personal story, just as her husband’s public statements are part of the national immigration debate. Her parents immigrated to this country seeking opportunity just as mine did.

For Indians, the phrase indentured servant is not an ordinary political insult. During British colonial rule, millions of Indians were transported to plantations and other destinations under indenture agreements. Many endured harsh conditions, restricted freedom and systematic exploitation.

Although indenture was not identical to slavery, it was a coercive labor system whose legacy continues to shape the history of the Indian diaspora. To apply that terminology indiscriminately to Indian professionals who come to America to work, innovate and build their futures trivializes that history. Calling Indians indentured servants is highly offensive.

The H-1B program, despite its shortcomings, is not a system of indenture. It is a temporary employment-based visa program designed to enable American employers to recruit foreign professionals for specialized occupations.

Workers can face real vulnerabilities because their immigration status is connected to qualifying employment, particularly when they lose their jobs and must find another employer within the time allowed by immigration rules. Those vulnerabilities deserve serious attention. They do not, however, make every H-1B employee an indentured servant.

I have employed H-1B professionals from India for more than two decades, including during nearly 15 years running a software company. I have seen the value these professionals bring to American businesses, from their technical capabilities to their ability to solve difficult problems under demanding conditions.

Indian professionals have helped advance America’s technology, medicine, scientific research and entrepreneurial sectors. American businesses recruit these professionals because they possess skills and experience that employers value. That does not mean every foreign candidate is more qualified than an American applicant, nor does it mean every employer uses the visa program responsibly. It means the discussion should be based on evidence rather than stereotypes.

Vance’s concerns about American workers deserve examination. If a company lays off domestic employees while using immigration programs to obtain less expensive replacements, regulators should investigate whether the employer has complied with applicable laws and program requirements.

But layoffs occurring alongside H-1B employment do not by themselves establish that visa-holders replaced American workers or that a company acted unlawfully. The facts matter. Allegations must be tested against evidence.

There are also genuine abuses within the recruitment system. There have been legitimate concerns involving fabricated résumés, exaggerated experience, deceptive staffing practices and candidates whose qualifications did not match the positions they were hired to fill. Such practices harm American workers, undermine legitimate Indian professionals and erode public confidence in the program. Employers and staffing firms that knowingly misrepresent qualifications should face meaningful consequences.

The solution is a more accountable system, with credible verification of qualifications, transparent compensation, fair recruitment practices and rigorous enforcement against employers and intermediaries that circumvent the rules. Immigration policy should protect the integrity of American hiring without treating nationality as evidence of wrongdoing.

The U.S. has every right to prioritize its domestic workforce. But it should do so through sound policy rather than language that diminishes the dignity of the people who contribute to its economy.

This is why I would ask Mrs. Vance to speak up, not to defend every aspect of the H-1B program or to disagree with her husband for the sake of doing so, but to affirm a principle that should transcend partisan politics. We can acknowledge the failures of a visa program without accepting language that confuses employment dependence with servitude.

America’s strength has always depended, in part, on its ability to attract people who want to contribute their knowledge, ambition and labor. Indian professionals are part of that story. They are physicians treating patients, engineers developing technology, researchers pursuing discoveries and entrepreneurs creating businesses. They are also parents, citizens, neighbors and colleagues whose lives cannot be reduced to the terms of a visa.

Mrs. Vance has her own voice and must decide how to use it. But this moment offers an opportunity to remind the country that respect for American workers need not come at the expense of respect for Indian professionals.

Indians are not indentured servants. They are professionals who come to America to work, contribute and pursue opportunities. The answer to an imperfect immigration system is to fix its flaws, not demean the people who participate in it.

Sreedhar Potarazu, MD, MBA, is an author, board-certified ophthalmologist and clinical director at American Eye Care.

articles.title: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectile, Singapore says
articles.summary: All 21 sailors on the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride were evacuated safely after it was hit by an projectile on Tuesday, maritime authorities say.
articles.body:
A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities.

All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said.

Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water.

The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula.

Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday.

Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added.

Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.

At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization.

The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time.

However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency.

One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping.
