articles.title: How Lebanon can be Trump’s first success in a troubled region
articles.summary: Following a June 2026 trilateral agreement aimed at disarming Hezbollah and restoring Lebanese sovereignty, author David Hale argues that increased American involvement and persistent diplomatic pressure are necessary to maintain momentum and prevent regional instability.
articles.body:
The Trump administration has done more than any of its predecessors to restore sovereignty for a much traumatized nation, Lebanon. The Israel Defense Forces’ operations in 2024 against Hezbollah decimated that organization, long the “A Team” in global terror.

With Lebanon no longer under the shadow of Iranian and Hezbollah dominance, a pro-sovereignty Lebanese president and prime minister came to office. They want to do what none of their predecessors would do: restore the Lebanese state’s monopoly of arms and control of its borders, regain power from Iran’s proxy, and remove from Tehran the decisions of war and peace in Lebanon.

America followed up in June 2026 with a trilateral framework agreement for a phased, conditions-based approach to disarming Hezbollah and restoring Lebanese control over all its territory, including in the South. Moreover, it placed on the horizon a future of peaceful relations between Lebanon and Israel, ending a cycle of violence that locked these two nations into the conflicts of others — the PLO, Syria and Iran. Despite the ups and downs of conflict and diplomacy elsewhere in the Middle East, representatives of Lebanon, Israel and America have met regularly to fulfill this promise.

While Lebanon offers a bright point of hope, the excellent groundwork laid by the Trump initiative is losing momentum. It is not because of a lack of goodwill, but an absence of persistent, high-level, intense action by all concerned.

During ten days in Beirut and Jerusalem, I heard growing public support for this process. Polling in Lebanon shows that taboos about disarming Hezbollah and peace with Israel are fast eroding. Hezbollah’s standing in its own Shia community has evaporated. Its discredited leaders tried to incite civil war to defeat the June trilateral agreement; no one answered the call. It is a fluid situation, and the Lebanese state — mostly absent from the South for nearly 50 years — should fill the vacuum now.

Despite these promising conditions, implementation has been leisurely. The recent Israeli release of low-security Lebanese prisoners helped, and the Lebanese are making a good faith effort to locate the remains of Israeli soldiers lost in battle in Lebanon. More gestures would help demonstrate the benefits of peace.

The Israeli government has said it ended its military operations in the South and begun to re-deploy some soldiers to Israel. The lesson of Israel’s unilateral withdrawals from Lebanon and Gaza a generation ago is the imperative of handing over to a partner. The trilateral framework calls for that, with Israel clearing Hezbollah out of pilot zones and bringing the Lebanese Army in as it pulls out, with an international verification structure assessing the process.

Yet, three months after the agreement, Israel has not handed any more territory to the Lebanese, nor has a verification team arrived. Israel’s enlightened self-interest is to bolster the credibility of the Lebanese Army with the phased withdrawals it agreed to in June. Israel’s election and coalition formation process — with little chance of a government emerging until mid-December — limits options. Nonetheless, diplomatic momentum in preserving Israel’s security gains is essential.

While getting the pilot zone methodology back on track, there is no reason for the Lebanese Army to refrain from regaining the monopoly of arms elsewhere. Hezbollah does not fear the Lebanese Army. Its leaders and their Iranian masters assess that the army is cautious and that they can outwait Israel and America. That must change.

The burden is on Israel and Lebanon, but a stronger American presence on the ground is indispensable, separate from the verification process. A modest number of embedded American soldiers can advise and assist the Lebanese Army at the brigade command level. They will not be in harm’s way, as they will be protected by Lebanese soldiers. It will strengthen the Lebanese Army as it restores sovereignty and allow Americans to assess and advise directly how best the Lebanese Army can act on its own and expunge any residual Hezbollah influence.

American ambassadors in Jerusalem and Beirut have critical roles to play, but trilateral negotiations cannot be handled by them alone. A full-time envoy should be on the doorsteps of leaders in those two countries every week, pushing, prodding, assessing, listening, and overcoming obstacles. That team should also enlist Arab and European support not just for the Lebanese Army, but to help the state repair south Lebanon as an alternative to Iranian funding.

The best thing America can do is keep the pressure on Iran. As the U.S. constrains Iran, Hezbollah is feeling the pain. But it is not just a question of squeezing our adversaries economically. Lebanese will watch closely which way the power balance between America and Iran lands during the remainder of the Trump administration, and adjust their expectations accordingly.

Washington is closer than ever to ending the cycles of violence generated by Iran and its proxies that have destroyed so much of the Middle East. Combined pressure on our adversaries, and support for leaders in Israel and Lebanon seeking to achieve peace, require persistence and active measures. With redoubled effort, Lebanon can be Trump’s first success in a troubled region.

David Hale is a Distinguished Diplomatic Fellow at the Middle East Institute. Hale previously served as U.S. Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon, and Special Envoy for Middle East Peace.

articles.title: In cigarette-butt asphalt tests, researchers found a 1.5% filter-waste blend gave the mix its best resistance to permanent deformation
articles.summary: Researchers discover that a 1.5% blend of cigarette butt waste in asphalt provides optimal resistance to permanent deformation, offering a sustainable solution to road construction and waste management.
articles.body: Researchers have tested cigarette-butt waste as an ingredient in asphalt mixtures, with one study finding that a mix that contained 1.5% cigarette butts had the lowest flow value among the tested concentrations, which indicates the strongest resistance to deformation by that measure. The same study found that increasing the cigarette-butt content changed the mixture's behavior under load, although its separate high-temperature rutting test produced a different optimum.The work examined cigarette butts as a waste material that could be incorporated into bituminous road mixtures, and researchers prepared samples with different amounts of cigarette butts and measured properties including Marshall stability, flow and resistance to deformation. Most conventional filters are made from cellulose acetate, which is a form of plastic-like cellulose that does not readily break down in the environment. Cigarette butts that have been used can also contain residual tobacco, tar and other substances, which has made their disposal an environmental problem. A later review of cigarette-butt asphalt research noted that researchers have investigated several ways of encapsulating or incorporating the waste into pavement materials.The 1.5% mix behaved differently under loadResearchers first tested cigarette-butt contents of 1%, 3% and 5% in the 2018 experiment, and the 3% mixture produced serious segregation, so the researchers tested lower concentrations of 1%, 1.5% and 2%. The Marshall test was then used to assess the mixtures, following which researchers reported that the 1.5% mixture had the lowest flow value among the tested cigarette-butt concentrations. In asphalt testing, flow is related to the amount of deformation that occurs under the Marshall loading conditions, and the paper therefore identified 1.5% as the best proportion for anti-deformation performance based on that measurement.In another study, the researchers examined high-temperature performance using a wheel-tracking or rutting test, and the dynamic stability increased as the cigarette-butt content increased, with the 2% mixture recording the highest dynamic stability in that experiment. “Best resistance to deformation” can refer to different measurements, as the 1.5% result came from the flow-value comparison, while the 2% result came from the high-temperature dynamic-stability test, and the study did not establish that 1.5% was universally the optimum concentration for every form of pavement deformation.Researchers have tested several ways to use the wasteOne investigation that was published in Construction and Building Materials examined cigarette butts that were encapsulated in bitumen before they were incorporated into stone mastic asphalt. That research found improved Marshall stability in mixtures that contained 1% and 2% encapsulated cigarette butts and reported increased resistance to permanent deformation, which is important because cigarette filters can contain substances that may leach out. The researchers therefore also examined leachate from the asphalt mixtures rather than treating the waste simply as an inert filler.A larger review of waste fibres in asphalt has since placed cigarette-butt materials among several experimental additives that are being investigated for pavement applications. The research has included whole cigarette butts encapsulated in asphalt, shredded filter fibres and other processed forms, with different studies having used different concentrations and testing methods, so their results cannot simply be combined into one recommended percentage.The 1.5% finding therefore belongs to a specific laboratory study and a specific performance measurement, and it does not mean that roads containing exactly 1.5% cigarette-butt waste have been proven to outperform conventional asphalt in real-world traffic. The research instead shows that a small proportion of cigarette-butt waste can alter the mechanical behavior of an asphalt mixture under controlled testing.You use AI every day. articles.title: Zelensky says ‘people will die’ because of Starlink decision
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned there could be dire consequences after his government reported that its air defense mechanisms had been mired by unannounced limitations on SpaceX satellites. Zelensky, in an interview Wednesday with Piers Morgan, called the slowdown of the company’s Starlink services a “big mistake.” “People will die, of course, if attacks will…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned there could be dire consequences after his government reported that its air defense mechanisms had been mired by unannounced limitations on SpaceX satellites. Zelensky, in an interview Wednesday with Piers Morgan, called the slowdown of the company’s Starlink services a “big mistake.”

“People will die, of course, if attacks will continue and if Starlink will not work … it’s not helpful,” he said.

The Ukrainian leader added that he hopes the limitation was only a “mistake,” suggesting it was “maybe a huge technical problem” at SpaceX.

A source familiar told The Hill on Wednesday that Starlink services were cut off for objects that traveled more than 100 miles an hour, impacting the capabilities of Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters.

The disruption followed the Trump administration’s threats to cut off U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine and the decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel amid sky-high fuel costs.

When pressed by Morgan about whether he felt “betrayed” by President Trump’s deal with Russia, the Ukrainian leader replied, “Really, yes.”

“It’s more complicated than just my emotions or just my feelings,” he added. “Yes, it depends not on me. Our country has to survive.”

Zelensky said it was “a pity” Ukraine is losing the U.S. as a “strong partner” in its military operations against Russia, which have lasted more than four years .

“It’s not about business for us,” he said. “It’s just our life, and this is our country, it’s our body, our home, our children and this is very important for us.”

“That’s why it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side, but we are OK that he’s in the middle,” the Ukrainian president continued. “But if you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle, not on the wrong side. … This is not [the] right side of history.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House and SpaceX for comment.

Morgan’s full interview with Zelensky will air Wednesday evening.
